title: Those sent forth
hookLine: by the winds sent forth one after another (77:1)

lines: A SURAH, FRESH FROM HIS MOUTH.
A SNAKE, AND NO HARM DONE.
cards: A cave in Mina, outside Mecca. A small group sits with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.
Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, one of his companions, later remembered it: a new surah was coming down, and Ibn Mas'ud was taking it fresh from the Prophet's mouth. Then a snake slid out of the rock.
The Prophet told them to kill it. They rushed it, and it got away. And he said, more or less: it was spared your harm, as you were spared its harm.
That's how al-Mursalat arrived, in a hadith in al-Bukhari. Surah seventy-seven opens with something that keeps coming.

teach.b: Wal-mursalati 'urfa. By those sent forth, one after another. Al-mursalat comes from the root r-s-l, to send, the same root as rasul, a messenger, and risalah, a message.
So the very first word of the surah is about sending. But sent forth what? The verse doesn't name them, and commentators read it in more than one way.
Some say the winds, gust after gust. Others say angels, sent down with Allah's commands.

teach.h: ONE AFTER ANOTHER, LIKE A MANE.
teach.b: Some held both together. 'Urfan has two readings as well: one after another, like the hairs of a horse's mane, also called 'urf, lying in a row; or with kindness, from the same letters as ma'ruf, the good and decent thing.
Then five oaths in a run: those sent forth, those that blow hard, those that spread, those that separate, those that bring down a reminder. Five lines that sound like weather rolling in.
Verse six says why the reminder comes: as an excuse or a warning. Verse seven lands the point: what you are promised will surely happen.
Before the surah says anything about the Day to come, it points at something you've felt on your face. Wind doesn't arrive once.
It keeps coming. The One who keeps sending the wind keeps sending reminders too.
Umm al-Fadl, the Prophet's aunt by marriage, said in another hadith that al-Mursalat was the last surah she heard him recite, at the sunset prayer, near the end of his life.
A surah about things that keep coming, and it kept being recited to the end.

how: Al-Mursalat is a short Meccan surah recited in prayer; commentators differ on whether its first verses describe winds, angels or both.

o: the scribes who first wrote down the Qur'an
the believers who travel on to Mecca
those sent forth, one after another

games.q: those sent forth — tap the pairs.
p: a messenger, from the same root
one after another, like a mane
heard it revealed in a cave at Mina

s: the surah names exactly what was sent forth
it doesn't. commentators read the winds, the angels, or both.
al-mursalat shares a root with rasul, messenger
both come from r-s-l, to send.
a hadith places its revelation in a cave at Mina
Ibn Mas'ud remembered it, and a snake that got away.

games.q: you're in the cave at Mina. the surah is being recited, and a snake slides out of the rock. the Prophet tells you to kill it. you rush it, and it escapes. what does he say?
o: it was spared your harm, as you were spared its harm.
games.why: in the hadith in al-Bukhari, once it has escaped, he says: it was spared your harm, as you were spared its harm.

practice: Listen for something that repeats: a fan, traffic, a clock, wind against a window, a neighbor's footsteps, or, if the room is silent, your own breath, coming in again without your asking.
Pick one and stay with it, and let each return count as one more arrival.

wordCard.voice: Al-mursalat. Those sent forth, one after another: angels or winds, the first word of surah seventy-seven, from the root of messenger. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic, 77:1: by those sent forth, one after another.

carryVoice: Your line: sent forth. Wind, breath and reminders never come just once. Day six hundred sixty-two.
